title: Microkernel Pattern
oneLiner: Keeps a minimal, stable core system, with all extended functionality added through independent, pluggable modules.

hero.name: The Core
hero.catchphrase: I stay small. Everything else plugs in.
hero.power: Keeps the central system deliberately minimal, letting all extended functionality live in independent plugins added without modifying the core itself.
hero.weakness: Plugin isolation and versioning is real engineering work — a poorly-isolated plugin can still destabilize the very core it was supposed to be independent from.
hero.origin: The Core appeared after a code editor's single monolithic binary had grown to include a spell-checker, three linters, and a git client baked directly in, making the whole app crash whenever any one of them had a bug.

story.problem: A code editor's core binary directly includes a spell-checker, three linters, and a git client. A crash in any one of them takes down the entire editor, and nobody can add a feature without touching the core.
story.solution: The Core strips the editor down to a minimal kernel: file editing, rendering, and a plugin API. The spell-checker, linters, and git client become independent plugins loaded through that API.
story.result: A buggy linter plugin can crash and be disabled without affecting the rest of the editor. New features ship as new plugins — the core itself barely changes.

before: All features are baked directly into one monolithic core
A bug in any feature can crash the entire application
Adding a feature means modifying the core system
after: The core stays minimal; features live in independent plugins
A buggy plugin can fail without crashing the core
Adding a feature means adding a new plugin, not touching the core

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A crash report shows the entire editor going down because of a bug in a third-party spell-checker built directly into the core.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The spell-checker crashed and took the whole editor down with it. Why does a spell-checker bug get to kill file editing?

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Core appears small and stable at the center, with slots around it waiting for plugins to snap in.
panels.speaker: The Core
panels.dialogue: I stay small on purpose. Everything else — spell-checking, linting, git — plugs into me. None of it lives inside me.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: The core exposes a stable plugin API. SpellCheckerPlugin, LinterPlugin, and GitPlugin each register independently.
panels.speaker: The Core
panels.dialogue: A plugin crashing is isolated to itself. The core — file editing, rendering — keeps running no matter what a plugin does.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The buggy spell-checker plugin now fails safely, disabled on its own, while the rest of the editor keeps working.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The spell-checker crashed and got disabled automatically. Everything else in the editor kept working the whole time.

useWhen: You're building a platform where third parties (or your own teams) need to add independent features without touching a shared core.
Different features have very different lifecycles, and coupling them to a monolithic release schedule is costly.
You want a failure in one feature to be isolated, not able to bring down the whole system.
avoidWhen: The application has a small, fixed feature set with no real need for extensibility.
The overhead of designing and maintaining a stable plugin API isn't worth it for your actual extensibility needs.
Plugin isolation can't be properly enforced in your platform/language, making 'independent' plugins a false promise.
commonMistakes: Designing a plugin API that's too narrow, forcing plugin authors to hack around it and reach into internals anyway.
Underestimating the engineering cost of true plugin isolation (sandboxing, versioning, failure containment).
Letting the 'core' quietly grow bloated over time by accreting features that should have been plugins from the start.
Not versioning the plugin API carefully, breaking third-party plugins on every core update.
explanation.realWorldExample: VS Code's extension system, Eclipse's plugin architecture, and browser extension APIs are all real-world Microkernel implementations — a minimal, stable core with rich functionality added entirely through independent plugins.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from just having a good plugin system?

conversation.speaker: The Core
conversation.message: A 'plugin system' bolted onto a monolith is easy to add and easy to compromise. My discipline is deeper — the CORE itself must stay genuinely minimal. If a feature isn't essential, it doesn't belong inside me at all.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the real cost of building me properly?

conversation.speaker: The Core
conversation.message: A stable, well-designed plugin API is hard to get right upfront, and true isolation — so a bad plugin can't crash me — takes real engineering. Skimp on either, and I'm just a monolith with extra steps.

codeBattle.scenario: Your team is building a browser where third-party developers need to add extensions (ad blockers, password managers, screenshot tools) without ever being able to crash the core browsing engine.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Core keeps the browsing engine minimal and stable, with every extension living as an isolated plugin that can fail without taking down the core.

quiz.question: What is the defining trait of a Microkernel architecture?
options: A minimal, stable core with all extended functionality added through independent plugins
A single monolithic binary containing every feature
A system with no core at all, only plugins
A database schema with many small tables
quiz.answer: A minimal, stable core with all extended functionality added through independent plugins
quiz.explanation: Deliberately keeping the core small, and pushing everything else out to plugins, is exactly what defines this pattern.

quiz.question: What's the key benefit of isolating features as plugins?
options: A bug in one plugin doesn't necessarily crash the entire application
It makes the application impossible to extend further
It removes the need for any core system at all
It guarantees the application will never have bugs
quiz.answer: A bug in one plugin doesn't necessarily crash the entire application
quiz.explanation: Failure isolation is one of Microkernel's biggest practical benefits over a monolithic design.

quiz.question: What's a real engineering challenge in implementing Microkernel well?
options: Designing a stable, well-versioned plugin API and enforcing genuine plugin isolation
quiz.answer: Designing a stable, well-versioned plugin API and enforcing genuine plugin isolation
quiz.explanation: Without real isolation and a stable API, the promised benefits of Microkernel don't actually materialize.

quiz.question: What's a well-known real-world Microkernel implementation?
quiz.explanation: VS Code's minimal core plus rich extension ecosystem is a textbook, widely-used example of Microkernel architecture.
